nodes.label: x86-64 port
nodes.rationale: The 64-bit-only line was drawn around word size rather than architecture precisely so a second instruction set would not be a refactor. All thirteen kernel/*.c compiled with no #ifdef; the userland needed six syscall stubs, an entry stub, a setjmp, two ring barriers and one #if. Four ARM habits proved silently wrong: hlt is not wfi, syscall saves only rcx/r11, the interrupted stack pointer is per-thread not per-CPU, and thread_tick only records without calling thread_preempt_if_needed.

nodes.label: hal/virtio (shared drivers)
nodes.rationale: The four virtio drivers - block, network, input, sound - moved rather than being rewritten, with each board bringing its own transport underneath: qemu-virt reads fixed offsets from a device-tree window, pc walks PCI capabilities across a BAR. The sequence is identical and every register is somewhere else. What is shared is the conversation, not the ring, because block chains descriptors, input hands over empty buffers and sound has four queues.

nodes.label: ramfb framebuffer
nodes.rationale: Chosen over virtio-gpu because hal_fb_init is 'ask the firmware for a linear framebuffer and let it say where the pixels are', which is what ramfb and the Pi mailbox both do. About a hundred lines against eight hundred for PCI enumeration plus virtqueues plus the virtio-gpu command set. virtio-gpu needs an explicit RESOURCE_FLUSH and is therefore the target that will earn the interface a hal_fb_flush, with two implementations in front of it rather than one. The stride is padded to 4160 bytes on purpose so that a wrong width*4 offset calculation cannot hide.

nodes.label: virtio_open / virtio_begin split
nodes.rationale: virtio_open reset a device it had only been asked to find, which is fine for a driver claiming the first card of its kind and wrong for input.c, which walks past devices to reach the one it wants. The tablet's scan reset the running keyboard. It worked on ARM by luck, because QEMU lays virtio-mmio windows out in reverse of the order devices are given. Discovery and claiming are two calls now.

nodes.label: sched_prio.c - five priority bands
nodes.rationale: Strict priority with immediate preemption, borrowed from QNX: idle, low, normal, display, input, round robin inside each, and a thread that becomes ready while outranking the running one takes the CPU at the next exception. Not taken from QNX: 256 levels and hard guarantees. Starvation is real under strict priority and accepted deliberately. The first version scanned eight levels and cost twice as much; an occupancy bitmask plus clz makes the pick one instruction.

nodes.label: struct scheduler policy seam
nodes.rationale: thread.c owns the mechanism and struct scheduler owns which runnable thread runs next, so a different algorithm is a new file. Per-thread policy state is embedded in struct thread rather than reached through a pointer, because there is no allocator to hand a policy its own storage. Swapping policies at runtime had to drain rather than reset: sched_use calls init, which empties the queues, so threads are pulled out one at a time and handed to the new policy with interrupts masked.

nodes.label: Priority inheritance across IPC
nodes.rationale: From QNX, and it fits a synchronous rendezvous exactly because the kernel already knows who is blocked on whom. It answers the failed experiment of promoting the console server to the input band, which starved the machine since that process is also the output path. A server sits at NORMAL and becomes urgent for exactly as long as something urgent waits on it. Cleared on reply rather than unwound, erring downward, which is the safe direction. Costs context_switch +9.0% and ipc_roundtrip +13.7%, not recorded as a new baseline because whether that is worth paying is a decision rather than a measurement.

nodes.label: Lazy FP/SIMD save
nodes.rationale: The switch disarms FP (CPACR_EL1.FPEN) and the first floating-point instruction traps into fp_fault, which swaps the register file. context_switch -29.9% and ipc_roundtrip -16.2%, against exception +4.3% for one comparison per exception. Trapping EL0 alone was tried and three tests said no: kernel threads run at EL1 and longjmp writes d8-d15 from its buffer, so arming both levels is simpler than either. The kernel being -mgeneral-regs-only is what makes every kernel thread free.

nodes.label: Synchronous IPC (SYS_CALL / SYS_RECEIVE / SYS_REPLY)
nodes.rationale: There is no asynchronous send, so every message to a server blocks for its reply by construction. This is why triple buffering cannot remove the wait on commit, and why a non-blocking send is a change to the IPC model rather than a local optimisation.

nodes.label: ipc_receive with a deadline
nodes.rationale: A server that sleeps on a timer is deaf: the audio server could not answer a client until the timer came round, so Music played at two thirds speed with the processor almost idle. Slow and idle at the same time means waiting on the wrong thing. Both halves already existed - THREAD_BLOCKED and thread_wake_sleepers - and had never been put together. Writing the test found a real race: unlinking the timed-out receiver after it woke left a window where a sender was handed a receiver that had given up, so ipc_timed_out now unlinks before the thread becomes runnable.

nodes.label: Non-blocking send (planned)
nodes.rationale: Half a browser frame is the application blocked on a commit whose handler swaps an index and records a rectangle. Needs a new syscall, a fixed-size queue in the endpoint struct because the kernel has no allocator, a decision about what a full queue does (dropping a stale commit for the newest is right for a compositor), and backpressure so an application cannot get more than two frames ahead.

nodes.label: Per-thread capability table (32 slots)
nodes.rationale: Sixteen slots was a number from when the userland was a shell; a graphical application holds its console, its /dev/wm endpoint, the filesystem, its window's region, a read buffer, decode buffers and a region per embedded font. Raising it to 64 panicked the benchmark image because a slot is 32 bytes and the thread stacks must stay inside the first 2 MB of RAM. Settled at 32, with SYS_ERR_NO_CAPS as its own error rather than folded into NO_ROOM.

nodes.label: region_of index-cache bug
nodes.rationale: region_of in sys_user.c cached mappings keyed by capability index, safe only while an index was never reused - which was true until sys.release existed. Afterwards a server dropped slot 1, the next region arrived at slot 1, and the cache handed back the previous region's address. Found by making the server read back its own write; three plausible hypotheses were tested and discarded first.

nodes.label: memobj - a region is a list of pages
nodes.rationale: Contiguous regions could fail to allocate on a fragmented machine even with memory free; memobj.h had named that cost in its own words and it became real, so the premise changed. A page holds 512 pointers and the index is allocated per region that exists, so .bss goes from 10 KB to 24 KB rather than a quarter of a megabyte. Given up: mapping walks an index, and a region can no longer be handed to a device expecting one physical run - nothing does, since DMA uses identity-mapped kernel buffers.

nodes.label: memobj_unref / memobj_create slot races
nodes.rationale: Found by a review pass reading the code as it now is rather than remembering writing it. memobj_unref cleared in_use before walking the index to free pages, so another sys.memory could claim the descriptor and rewrite index[] mid-walk; memobj_create mirrored it. Turning a region into a page list widened a window the contiguous code had narrowly. The slot is claimed first and released last now.

nodes.label: USER_SHARE_VA - a separate window for shared regions
nodes.rationale: A range is what says who frees the pages. Shared regions in the SYS_MAP window meant two processes freed one region's pages twice on exit; the panic was the lucky half, since SYS_UNMAP would silently have created a use-after-free. Fixed with a second window rather than a per-page owner flag, so the check is where the addresses come from rather than a bit they carry. Shared pages are charged to whoever created the region, not to each mapper.

nodes.label: SYS_SLEEP / thread_sleep_until
nodes.rationale: Yielding in a loop is a spin. The audio path had two, and playing a tone cost 63% of the machine for the client and 26% for the server against 8% for Doom. Exposing thread_sleep_until, which the kernel had had since M6 behind SYS_WAIT_INPUT's console check, took the same tone under 1%.

nodes.label: SYS_WAIT_INPUT
nodes.rationale: Lets the one process allowed to read input sleep until there is some, with the virtio input interrupt cutting the sleep short. An idle desktop went from ninety-six per cent to one.

nodes.label: SYS_SYSINFO
nodes.rationale: Hands back raw ID registers and pool counts and decodes nothing, so the tables that turn 0x410fd083 into Cortex-A72 live in Lua and a processor the kernel has never heard of is described without the kernel changing. struct sysinfo never being zeroed was a security bug wearing the same clothes as the two-copies-of-one-fact shape: any field the kernel does not write is kernel stack handed to a process.

nodes.label: SYS_SCHED_INFO / SYS_SCHED_SET
nodes.rationale: Quantum and policy are anyone's to change because tuning the machine you are sitting at is not reaching into another process; priority is not, because bands are handed out by capability precisely so nothing can promote itself, and a syscall for it would undo that in one line.

nodes.label: TICK_HZ = 250
nodes.rationale: The sound device chose it: four measurements delivering 580 ms of audio showed that buffering more does not help, because the shortfall is in how often the queue is topped up rather than how much it holds. A 5.8 ms period cannot be serviced on a 10 ms clock. Everything measured in ticks changed meaning with it, and the blinking cursor is how that got found - CURSOR_TICKS = 25 with a comment reading 'at 100 Hz', and behind it both schedulers' quantum as a bare 10.

nodes.label: Binned, growing malloc
nodes.rationale: malloc was a first-fit scan over one list holding every block, free or allocated, so an allocation cost what the heap already contained. Free blocks are binned by size class with the bin links inside each free block's own payload, which costs nothing because the minimum payload is exactly two pointers. alloc_table 79x faster; serialize fell 40% untouched. The heap also grows by asking the kernel for another arena, which retires the DOOM=1 heap flag. The trap written into the code: sys_map never reuses an address, so arenas are not adjacent and each must be its own physical list with NULL at both ends.

nodes.label: Read-only image mapped rather than copied
nodes.rationale: Code, fonts, icons and the Lua source of every program - 2.8 MB - are one set of physical pages for the machine, read-only and executable at EL0. Permissions live in the mapping rather than in the page, so nothing about isolation changes. A process holds 2224 KB where it held 7232; a whole desktop with a 3D cube holds 47 MB where it held 148. The test had to be rewritten: 'separate address spaces' checked that two processes' code was a different physical page, which was a proxy for isolation and is now deliberately false.

nodes.label: ADDRSPACE_MAX - the pool nothing counted
nodes.rationale: Spawning failed at eleven processes with every reported pool showing plenty free. A limit nothing counts is a limit nobody can find. Now 32, with as_count()/as_total() reported by SYS_SYSINFO, and tied to PROCESS_MAX by a test rather than by an include, because arch/ must not include a kernel header.

nodes.label: Intermittent panic in prio_pick_next
nodes.rationale: head[level] was NULL while the occupied bitmask said the level had somebody in it. Not root-caused. The queue invariant has only three writers and they look locally consistent, so the next place to look is a thread whose effective band changes while it is queued: thread_inherit and thread_disinherit write sched.effective, which is what level_of reads, and neither re-queues.

nodes.label: A yielding thread at NORMAL is starved
nodes.rationale: With ordinary programs at NORMAL instead of DISPLAY, a thread that spins on sys.yield() instead of blocking never advances while the desktop runs - the loop moves only when it makes an IPC call. Invisible until now because every program was promoted into the compositor's band, so nothing had ever run at NORMAL. This blocks the screen-grant fix.

nodes.label: Every launched program is handed the screen
nodes.rationale: Both launchers say may_pass_screen() and SPAWN_SCREEN or 0, so any program gets process_grant_screen - which maps the framebuffer into its address space and promotes it to SCHED_PRIO_DISPLAY. Two unintended consequences: any program can draw over the desktop without going near the window manager, which is ambient authority in a system whose first principle forbids it; and the compositor's band means nothing when everything is in it.

nodes.label: audio server
nodes.rationale: 482 lines of Lua became 462 of C plus a 108-line header. main.c dispatches role 16 before the interpreter is opened, so the process serving /dev/audio has no lua_State at all - the difference between promising not to allocate and being unable to. It did not change the underrun count, which was predicted; what it bought is that the audio path can no longer acquire a collector by accident.

nodes.label: devices server (/dev)
nodes.rationale: Does not list console, and that is the point: /dev/console is mounted to the console server, longest prefix wins, so a read of that path means give me a line of input. The first version listed it anyway and the devices command dutifully read it, so the console server swallowed the next thing typed. Listing a name you do not answer for is a lie.

nodes.label: console server
nodes.rationale: The interesting conversion: it is the one protocol with two implementations, since a terminal window mounts itself as its child's /dev/console and the runner that mounts it cannot tell which it got - the capability discipline working correctly. So the layout is compiled once into a kit and both sides go through it. read also stopped blocking inside a handler; the C server records who asked and answers from the loop.

nodes.label: ramfs (/data)
nodes.rationale: Converted to C so the system would be one thing rather than six servers in C and one in Lua for a feature's sake, at a price known in advance. Conversion found that /data had always stored Lua values rather than bytes, so the namespace packs and the server holds bytes with a flag. It also kept its store in .bss - static struct node nodes[128], 2.1 MB - so every process carried a copy of a server's private storage; it asks for the pages at startup now.

nodes.label: diskfs
nodes.rationale: The only Lua server left, and deliberately so: its core kfs.lua runs on the host as well as the guest, which is what lets make test check the filesystem format and the journal's power-loss window without booting a machine, at an instant a SIGKILL aimed at a running QEMU hits only by luck.

nodes.label: net server (Ethernet/ARP/IPv4/ICMP)
nodes.rationale: In C because it is a server on the packet path. Fragments and IP options are refused rather than half-handled. SPAWN_NET is the disk's grant pointed outwards - whoever can send a raw frame can claim any address and read every frame - so one process holds the card and /net is what everything else asks. A card is a device; a stack is someone you ask.

nodes.label: namespace kit (new_namespace)
nodes.rationale: A kit, not a server: it is run in the caller's own process, has no endpoint and no thread, and nobody asks it anything. Calling it a server was a documented error that an argument for converting four thousand lines was built on top of. The root of the namespace is the one thing no server can answer, because only the namespace knows what has been attached to it and where.

nodes.label: init and supervision
nodes.rationale: The kernel starts init and nothing else. It cannot promote a child beyond itself: a spawn resolves every capability against the parent's own table. Supervision is noticing rather than restarting - init waits and learns which child ended with what code. It says why it could not start something, because a process that dies takes its own error message with it, and init is the only one left who knows.

nodes.label: Declared shape (struct protocols)
nodes.rationale: A server receives exactly what it expects, not whatever somebody put in a table: a fixed-field struct means most wrong shapes cannot be expressed, so the wire refuses them and the server never has to check. audioproto.h, devproto.h, binproto.h, appproto.h and conproto.h are the headers both sides compile against. The cost is real - editing a header and rebuilding both sides, and errors are numbers - and it moved the collector out of the server and into every client on the frame path until con.wait did the exchange in C.

nodes.label: audioproto.h
nodes.rationale: The first declared-shape protocol header. Its layout is written twice, in C and as a string.pack format, which is the one place serialize.h's one-implementation rule is deliberately bent - a _Static_assert, a load-time assert and a server length check stand where the shared implementation used to.

nodes.label: Spleen 8x16 bitmap font
nodes.rationale: BSD-2-Clause, vendored unmodified beside its licence and converted by tools/bdf2c.py into 96 glyphs of sixteen bytes - one byte per row, MSB leftmost, the VGA ROM layout, which makes drawing a glyph a shift and a test rather than a lookup. Linux's font_8x16.c was rejected because it is GPL and would have made the kernel image GPL. It has ASCII and nothing else, which is why accented Latin still draws boxes.

nodes.label: IBM Plex outline faces
nodes.rationale: Every file in assets/fonts/ was -Regular, so <strong> and <em> could only ever have rendered as nothing. Four Plex weights joined them - Sans Bold, Italic, BoldItalic and Mono Bold, OFL - and dropping them in broke font resolution silently.

nodes.label: audioring.h - SPSC period ring
nodes.rationale: Replaced a 1024-byte period travelling as a message payload 172 times a second, which manufactured 340 KB/s of garbage inside a 5.8 ms deadline. It happened because MSG_BYTES is 2048 and a period is 1024 - it fit, and fitting is the trap.

nodes.label: tcpring.h - two SPSC rings in a shared region
nodes.rationale: Written down before a byte moved rather than after somebody found a message worked for the first ten kilobytes. The receive window is the ring's free space, not a number the stack invented - a window is a promise, and a client that stops reading really does slow the sender down.

nodes.label: Control by message, data by shared memory
nodes.rationale: A message says what to do; a region holds what to do it to. The test is the rate: if it recurs because the hardware says so - a frame, a period, a packet, a block - the bytes live in a region and the message carries only where and how much. Learned expensively from the audio server. The discipline that comes with it is single-producer single-consumer rings with indices.

nodes.label: Single-producer single-consumer ring
nodes.rationale: One side only writes, one side only reads, nobody takes a lock, and the indices are the only thing both touch. Anything that wants more than that wants a message.

nodes.label: Capabilities by index, no global names
nodes.rationale: A capability travels out of band, never inside the serialised bytes: an index means something only in the table it came from, so the kernel translates on delivery and what arrives is the receiver's own index. Stored as index plus one so that zero means none. No capability leaves the namespace - there is deliberately no fs.capability.

nodes.label: C is what runs for another process, Lua for a person
nodes.rationale: The line is a layer rather than a judgement, because a judgement has to be made again at every new subsystem by somebody who remembers. The audio server is what the judgement cost. The argument for C is jitter rather than speed: structure-shaped Lua costs about 2%, and what decides a server is gc_pause_max at about 1.25 ms against a 16 ms frame. What keeps a policy server in Lua is the shape of its bug - a Lua server cannot have a buffer overflow, and one bug is a stack trace and the other is an evening.

nodes.label: Hot reload (removed)
nodes.rationale: It was real - M5 proved it with a server's code replaced mid-conversation - and it worked because state and behaviour are separate: serve takes a factory, so anything in state survives and anything captured in a closure is lost. Then the disagreement stopped happening because the servers ran out; ramfs was the last one that could be reloaded, and converting it deleted ROLE_RELOAD. Do not describe it as a tiebreaker any more. What survives is the shape, and level 2 where a supervisor restarts a server that died.

nodes.label: /kits/web
nodes.rationale: The whole libc bill for a hundred and forty thousand lines of HTML parser, CSS engine and DOM came to three functions: bsearch, strtoul and time. That was the question Tier 0 existed to answer - whether this libc holds up under serious third-party C.

nodes.label: /kits/pdf (pdftok.c)
nodes.rationale: The scanner is C and the profile is why: a page cost 1.1 seconds of which 538 ms was the tokenizer, at 144 microseconds a token, because string.sub allocates a one-character string per byte. In C the same 3,657 tokens take 4.7 ms. Not that C is faster, but that a scanner is the kind of thing where 110x is available and nothing is given up.

nodes.label: /kits/gl
nodes.rationale: A GL context costs ten bytes a pixel out of a two-megabyte heap. TinyGL asserts rather than returning when an allocation fails, and an assert here is a panic, so the kit refuses a context it cannot afford and says what would fit. The budget is three quarters of the heap, measured rather than chosen: half was tried first and would have refused a size that demonstrably worked, which is the more annoying way to be wrong about a limit because it looks like caution.

nodes.label: gfx (surface primitives)
nodes.rationale: A surface is a userdata over flat bytes; every pixel loop is in user/lib/gfx.c and every primitive clips rather than raising, because a window half off the edge of the screen is the normal case. No line of Lua computes a pixel offset - a pitch bug is invisible from inside the process and the whole suite passes with it, so the check has to live outside the guest in make screenshot.

nodes.label: gfx_draw.h - lending drawing to another kit
nodes.rationale: The surface stays an opaque pointer, so unlike docfont.c - which repeats struct surface's first four fields and says in a comment that two files must now agree - there is nothing to agree about. gfx_draw_text takes an outline face only and draws nothing without one, because silently substituting a size would make every line of a page the wrong height. Ascent is exposed separately from height because two faces on one line share a baseline rather than a top edge.

nodes.label: Face pool keyed by family, weight, slant, size
nodes.rationale: gfx held one face per role and there were four roles, so a heading could not be larger than a paragraph on the same screen - which made 'headings are larger' a gfx change rather than something a layout engine could express. Faces are a pool now, and the same name and size hands back the same face rather than rasterising 95 glyphs again. Continuous CSS sizes are rounded to a ladder so they cannot fill the pool.

nodes.label: UI kit (lib/ui.lua)
nodes.rationale: A view tree with nested coordinates and real clipping, follow modes, and widgets. Drawing produces commands, never pixels, so a view's list can be resent without re-running its handler.

nodes.label: docfont.c - fonts from inside a document
nodes.rationale: A font loaded from bytes in the document, rasterised by glyph index rather than codepoint, cached per face per size, with a draw that takes a whole page as a flat array so a page is two or three crossings instead of two thousand. A CID-keyed subset has no cmap and that is correct, so ensure_cmap writes a 22-byte table into our own copy and repoints the unused post entry at it rather than touching vendored stb_truetype.

nodes.label: g3d.lua - software 3D
nodes.rationale: surface:triangle is the only new C, because it runs once per pixel; the matrices, projection, back-face test and depth sort are Lua because they run once per vertex. A cube is 12 triangles and tens of thousands of pixels. Face winding is computed by g3d.orient rather than written by hand, because a cube with four faces wound wrong shows four faces at once and neither that nor the all-backwards version is visible in a screenshot.

nodes.label: minimp3 (vendored)
nodes.rationale: The first thing brought in here that needed no patches at all - no libm, no allocation, sixteen-bit output by default. NEON is safe because fp.S saves the whole q0-q31 file rather than the callee-saved half. One 256-frame period costs 0.095 ms to decode against a 5.8 ms deadline.

nodes.label: Vendored code is not modified
nodes.rationale: What is in the tree should be what the author released, and everything done to it should be a build step somebody can read. It decided the ensure_cmap fix in our own copy of a font rather than patching stb_truetype, and the -fcommon flag on vendored files only when libcss's stray _ALIGNED parsed as 180 definitions of one file-scope variable - upstream's latent bug, not Kosmos's.

nodes.label: browser (browser.lua)
nodes.rationale: The shape is the one the tree already uses twice: the engine is C behind use("/kits/web") and the application is Lua - window, chrome, history, scroll offset, navigation policy. It opens on a page compiled into browser.lua, because an operating system has no business asking the computer running it to start a web server, and every browser ever written ships a start page. An address beginning with a slash is read from the namespace rather than fetched.

nodes.label: web_style.c and the UA stylesheet
nodes.rationale: What was face_for() became a user-agent sheet at UA origin, which is how a browser has always expressed defaults and buys what a switch could not: an author writing h1 { font-size: 44px } wins, because the cascade already knows UA loses to author. No code knows that rule; libcss does. is_hidden's list of tag names became display:none on six selectors, so a page that hides something of its own is hidden too. Two special cases disappeared rather than being fixed. Inheritance is done by overwriting only what is specified, because overwriting unconditionally turns inheritance into its opposite.

nodes.label: The runs array (layout before paint)
nodes.rationale: One missing data structure was six missing features. Painting while walking the tree throws away where each word ended up, so nothing could be clicked, nothing could be bold inside a paragraph, and pre could not keep its spaces. Layout now produces positioned runs with a face, an ink and a link; paint is one loop over that array and knows nothing about the DOM, and hit testing is the same loop with a comparison instead of a draw. len == 0 is a rectangle, so painting stays one pass in layout order.

nodes.label: A box model (next)
nodes.rationale: Margins, padding, borders and width, which is what turns blocks stacked down the page into layout. Images and forms both wait on it. Layout will be ours rather than NetSurf's, because HTML5 error recovery and the CSS cascade are hopeless to hand-write - which is why the vendored libraries earn their place - while layout degrades gracefully; taking NetSurf's would mean taking its core for the part we can most afford to do simply.

nodes.label: css_computed_font_family NULL write
nodes.rationale: The generated getter stores the name list before it returns the keyword, so passing NULL is a write to address zero. It was far 0x0 at get_font_family on the first page rendered.

nodes.label: css_unit_len2device_px swapped arguments
nodes.rationale: css_fixed and css_unit are both integers, so nothing warned. It converted a length of CSS_UNIT_PX - zero - using a unit of 45056 and answered zero, and every size then fell through a range check to the inherited one. Colour and weight arrived from the cascade and only size did not, which is what made it findable.

nodes.label: font_short_name weight collision
nodes.rationale: Taking everything before the first dash was exactly right while every file ended -Regular.ttf. With a second weight present, Bold and Regular both became ibmplexsans, and FONT_FILES is sorted so Bold sorts first - the desktop's monospace font would quietly have become bold with no error anywhere. The name keeps the whole stem now and drops only -Regular, and font_asset tries exact matches before prefixes.

nodes.label: UTF-8 decoding in the text path
nodes.rationale: Each byte was cast to a codepoint, so a three-byte character became three lookups and three boxes; the built-in bitmap face's width function counted bytes, making one accented character two columns wide. gc:text also clipped with a byte slice where skip and room are counted in columns, which agreed only while everything on screen was ASCII. The mojibake recorded earlier was not a renderer bug at all: a test page with no meta charset produced a genuinely double-encoded document and the renderer drew what it was given - a false finding written down with confidence that survived a commit.

nodes.label: wm (window manager / compositor)
nodes.rationale: Its Lua half is about a ninth of a busy pass - composing 84.7% and already C, application requests 10.2%, polls 3.5% - so rewriting it in C would be four figures of lines for a fraction of a ninth. The profile answered the open question with no. What the same profile found instead was allocation: 4.2 KB of garbage a pass, 3.63 KB of it in wait_input, fixed by doing the exchange in C into a reused table. Window dragging is entirely inside wm, so no application waits during one.

nodes.label: Deskbar
nodes.rationale: It asks the window manager what is on screen rather than asking /app what registered, because a program that opens a window directly has one and no registration. Four sections - Applications, System, Preferences, Demos - because a preference is a choice that stays chosen, and the network configuration, process list, log and web server are windows onto services running right now.

nodes.label: Tracker
nodes.rationale: Finder's chrome: back and forward, a search box, a count. A plain word filters what is on screen; name:value is a query whose answer is a folder of files from all over the volume. A query result is refreshed twice a second rather than pushed, because the window is blocked in the desktop's poll and there is no way to wait on two things at once - and fs.poll does not help, because the two waits live in different servers, so a select over both would have to be something the namespace offers.

nodes.label: Terminal
nodes.rationale: It is a console server - it speaks the same write and read that /dev/console speaks and hands itself to its children under that name - which is the design working rather than a trick played on it. No program knows or can ask what is behind /dev/console. A window that is somebody's console cannot poll once a second, so ui has a poll_wait the Terminal sets to one tick.

nodes.label: Doom
nodes.rationale: Seven bugs on the way and the two the system owned are the ones to remember: snprintf ignored precision on integers, so %.3d of 33 gave 33 and the HUD font lumps came out one character short - a missing-file error caused by a formatting bug; and C output from a windowed process vanished entirely because SYS_WRITE is refused unless the process owns the console, so forty thousand lines started up, failed and said nothing.

nodes.label: httpd
nodes.rationale: nginx's shape - one process, an event loop, and a coroutine per connection - because there is no thread syscall at all: SYS_SPAWN makes a process, and a process has one lua_State, so two threads inside one would want a lock around the interpreter and would take turns anyway. The coroutine is why serve still reads as a straight line, with a yield wherever it used to wait.

nodes.label: webserver app
nodes.rationale: The manager is not the server and that is forced: accept blocks and a window that blocked would stop drawing. They talk through /data - the server writes its state and last forty lines, the manager reads them on a tick - which is a file rather than a message because the server has no idea anybody is watching.

nodes.label: about (About box)
nodes.rationale: The one live bug the 0.9 review found in prose that asserts hardware: it said 'a microkernel with a Lua userland, on AArch64' four lines above a Platform field reading QEMU q35 x86-64, so the window disagreed with itself in one screenful. It asks /dev/cpu now.

nodes.label: Replicants
nodes.rationale: One application publishes a view as source, state and a needs list, and another that has never heard of clocks adopts it and runs it. The replicant reports from inside its own environment what it could reach, which is the only honest place to ask.

nodes.label: Scripting architecture (/app)
nodes.rationale: An application answers for its own properties because it called ui.window, not because it has any scripting code. The registry hands out capabilities and never forwards, so one slow application cannot hold everyone else's door.

nodes.label: Drag and drop across windows
nodes.rationale: The desktop carries a kind and an opaque string it never reads, because it is the only process that knows what is under the pointer - a press grabs, so the destination never sees one. The reply is a one-shot right given to the window that was handed the drop and taken back after, so that telling the source is not a way to post an event to any window whose handle you can guess.

nodes.label: kfs (the filesystem format)
nodes.rationale: Borrowed, not invented: ext2's skeleton without block groups, which exist to keep inodes near data on a spinning disk and buy nothing on an SD card; ext3's journal with its space reserved from the start; BFS's attribute semantics; extents instead of indirect blocks. Written with string.pack so the format string beside the field names is the specification, and bounds-checked, which a C struct read off a disk is not. The superblock is written last, so an interrupted format leaves a disk that says it is not a filesystem, which is true.

nodes.label: The journal
nodes.rationale: ext3's shape: write the blocks into the journal, write one commit block, apply them, clear the header. The ordering is the whole guarantee. Each of the four rules was deleted in turn to check its test fails without it, and one did not, which is how a hole in the uncommitted-journal case was found. tools/test_kfs.lua tests replay by choosing the instant, because a SIGKILL cannot aim at the few milliseconds that matter.

nodes.label: Attributes and the index
nodes.rationale: One block per file, pointed at by the inode field reserved since the format was laid down. kind, size, mtime and the extent count are read from the inode and refused by setattr, because a stored copy of a fact is a copy that can disagree. The index is rebuilt at mount and nothing about it is written down: derived state that is also stored is state that can disagree with itself, and on a filesystem that disagreement is a query returning a file that is not there. name is indexed without anybody declaring it, which is BFS's rule.

nodes.label: Live queries
nodes.rationale: A watcher blocks in one call and the filesystem parks the reply until the answer changes - no timer, no repeated question.

nodes.label: Queries returned doubled paths on every real mount
nodes.rationale: One disk is mounted three times, so the namespace mapped /home/doc.pdf onto /home/doc.pdf in the server and then put the mount prefix back on the way out. And the server answered a question about /home with everything on the disk. Both survived because every query test used /data, the one mount with no root, so the two paths through that code had never both been walked. The new check reads a returned path back, because a doubled prefix is still a string and still looks like an answer.

nodes.label: tools/kfs.lua (host-side disk tooling)
nodes.rationale: The answer to the one real cost of not using FAT32 - a Mac cannot mount the image, but it can write it. One implementation of the format, not two, which is what makes it trustworthy.

nodes.label: read into / write from a region
nodes.rationale: read(fd, buf, n) with the buffer named by a capability instead of a pointer, because a server at EL0 cannot dereference the caller's pointer. Before it, nothing above about two kilobytes could be written at all. fs.write above two kilobytes reached sys.call and came back as an exception out of the serialiser - the same line working on one mount, failing with a sentence on another and throwing on a third, which is exactly the difference a namespace exists to hide.

nodes.label: The resource bug that appears on the Nth try
nodes.rationale: Three of the same shape: capability slots gone on the sixteenth read, a region per font per size, a process table full at round twenty-two, and diskfs keeping every region capability so the thirty-second large write failed with what reads like a bad pointer. This is why make stress exists and why the check is a loop of forty writes rather than one.

nodes.label: TCP
nodes.rationale: Three deliberate trades: one segment in flight retransmitted on a doubling timer, because a sliding window buys throughput on a long fat link and nothing on a line protocol; out-of-order segments dropped, which costs a retransmission and saves a reassembly buffer with an overlap policy, the well-known way to get a stack wrong; and the receive window is the ring's free space. Written down as not good: the local port is a counter, which an off-path attacker can guess, and there is no randomness here to do better with. A FIN is a wish, not an act - sending it while the ring still held bytes numbered it as if they did not exist.

nodes.label: fs.poll - the select this system wanted six times
nodes.rationale: Two masks, not one: a caller waiting to read wants to hear that bytes arrived, a caller waiting to write wants to hear that room appeared. One mask has to guess, and the version that guessed deadlocked - it reported a connection writable only when there was room and something still queued, so a client that acknowledged the whole ring left the server waiting for news that could no longer arrive.

nodes.label: SSH primitives
nodes.rationale: SHA-256, HMAC-SHA256, ChaCha20, Poly1305 and X25519, each against the vectors in its own specification. This is the one place in the project where a bug is silent rather than loud - a stack that gets a sequence number wrong stops working, and a cipher that gets a nonce wrong keeps working and is not secure - so 'it connected' is not evidence.

nodes.label: DNS resolver (next)
nodes.rationale: What stands between an address in four numbers and a name. With no TLS either, https is out; QEMU's NAT does give the guest real outbound internet, so a plain-HTTP host that serves by address works today.

nodes.label: tests/tests.c
nodes.rationale: 127 checks, 4,085 lines, the largest single test asset in the tree - and it has never run on x86-64, because there is no x86 test image target for TEST=1 to build. The suite that most directly exercises the kernel has run on one board only. Left open by the 0.9 review as real work rather than a line.

nodes.label: The display harness (62 display checks)
nodes.rationale: The measure worth quoting for the port, because it asks QEMU what is on the screen rather than asking the guest: the same sixty-two checks pass on x86-64 and aarch64 in about the same time.

nodes.label: Input delivered while the guest is busy (harness flakiness)
nodes.rationale: About one run in three fails, at three different phases, and every one is the same sentence: an input the harness sent did not arrive. Not one mechanism - the arrow goes through the monitor socket and virtio-input, Control-C down the serial line - so naming it 'the arrow key phase' was wrong. Ruled out: the arrow keys themselves, latency, and the shared monitor socket. The honest fix is probably a guest per phase and the honest measurement is a timestamp at each end rather than more repetitions.

nodes.label: make screenshot
nodes.rationale: Two halves of the display are tested and neither can prove the other: make test proves what the kernel wrote into its own memory and cannot prove a pixel ever reached a screen, so make screenshot asks QEMU through the monitor, on the far side of everything the kernel controls. Both were made to fail on purpose before being trusted.

nodes.label: make bench and baselines
nodes.rationale: QEMU numbers under -icount detect regressions rather than saying whether something is fast. The serialize benchmark is sensitive to what else is in the process rather than only to the serialiser, and has moved four times without anybody editing serialize.c - its note says to look at what was added to the process. A 'deadlock' once turned out to be a stale image: three conclusions were drawn from a binary nobody had rebuilt.

nodes.label: make stress
nodes.rationale: make test says the parts work and make screenshot says the machine works once; neither notices a pool that fills on the fiftieth try. So make release runs make stress, which uses the machine hard and then asks sysinfo whether it gave everything back.

nodes.label: make frames
nodes.rationale: Existed because nothing measured a frame: all five gated benchmarks are the kernel, in a system whose stated aim is a responsive desktop, so every argument about rewriting the window manager in C was an argument about a number nobody had. Its first run found the compositor filling the whole frame of every window a damage rectangle touched - ten pixels of damage costing 95,040. It also reports a KB/pass column per stage, which is what made the allocation finding visible.

nodes.label: run-kosmos.sh
nodes.rationale: Five bugs came out of one person trying to use it, and not one would have been found by any suite here - they were all in the layer nothing tests: the part a person types. It looked for the names a build tree has rather than the names a release has, did not look in build/, split a quoted -b argument because it was built as a string and expanded unquoted, matched a filename suffix the release had stopped using and exited rather than taking the best available, and never updated itself. It now also makes a 64 MB disk beside the image, because without one there is no filesystem at all.

nodes.label: get-and-run-kosmos.sh
nodes.rationale: sh -c "$(curl ...)" rather than curl | sh, and that is not style: a pipe is the script's stdin, and the last thing it does is hand over to QEMU with -serial mon:stdio. Checked rather than assumed.

nodes.label: tools/luacheck.c and luaglobals.py
nodes.rationale: luaglobals.py compares the globals each file reads against the environment it will run in, and exists because a lost local has killed a server four separate times.

nodes.label: tools/run_headless.py
nodes.rationale: Boots a machine with no display, which had silently stopped working: init asked for the screen grant whether or not there was a screen, the kernel refuses a grant it cannot give, and the refused spawn was the shell. It also now counts user/bin/*.lua on the host against ls /bin on the guest - two independent counts of the same thing, which is what makes it a check rather than a restatement of the code.

nodes.label: /bin reported 74 of its 82 programs
nodes.rationale: A listing reply holds BIN_CHUNK / BIN_NAME_MAX = 74 names and BIN_OP_LIST started at nought every time. The eight dropped were the last alphabetically and four were applications, so the Deskbar could not offer Tracker, the Terminal, the top bar or the web server. Nothing failed; the menu was just short. The guard was a _Static_assert that cannot check the number of programs, so it watched the chunk shrinking while the image grew past it.

nodes.label: Code has make test, prose has nobody
nodes.rationale: Every wrong thing the 0.9 review found was a sentence - in a comment, a string, a document or a Makefile variable - that was true when written and was never asked again. CLAUDE.md claimed a per-CPU struct, TPIDR_EL1 and a per-CPU runqueue, all three false since the repository's first commit: an intention written in the present tense before there was a kernel to describe. The port did not introduce these; it made them visible, because a second machine is a second reader. 43 AArch64 references remain in kernel/'s comments across nine files.

nodes.label: Doubled lists that nothing checks agree
nodes.rationale: X86_FLAGS against CFLAGS_BASE lost three things in a row, each found only when something broke - the user base address, the screen size, and the heap size. The last killed the TinyGL demos with a page fault at USER_HEAP plus exactly 512 pages, because the kernel mapped 512 and the userland compiled into it believed 3072.

nodes.label: Two copies of one fact that agree until they do not
nodes.rationale: One bug shape, five times in one session: the font role and the list selection, the bar's height and the height it was granted, USER_HEAP_PAGES in the kernel and USER_HEAP_SIZE in userland, appearance's hardcoded layout against a user-chosen font size, and struct sysinfo never being zeroed. A duration written as a count of ticks is the same shape - one fact stored twice - and nothing failed and no test caught any of the three ticks constants.

nodes.label: A test that exercises a different path from the user agrees with you
nodes.rationale: The arrow keys worked over the serial line and did nothing on a real keyboard, and every automated check typed over the serial line. A grep that kept only a summary threw away the failing run's output twice in one session. A check that cannot see a failure reports a pass: pdfview showed its error in the window and printed nothing, so grepping the serial log said every batch size worked. A test whose setup can quietly not happen - a yield with nothing else runnable does not switch - is a test that will one day pass for the wrong reason.

nodes.label: Slice-based edits silently delete code
nodes.rationale: Three times: nine test functions, then tests_run() and bench_run() - which read as make test hanging rather than failing - then run_program, which killed the shell silently because the shell prints by asking the console server. The rule is narrow anchors.

nodes.label: 3-4 audio underruns per 2.3 s (open)
nodes.rationale: Six structural changes did not move it: the shared ring, the priority band, an 8x buffer, the device interrupt, the C rewrite, and measuring during play rather than after. 194 interrupts per 400 periods means the device services about two periods per raise, which is QEMU's model rather than ours. The remaining question is a hardware question.

nodes.label: SMP (wanted)
nodes.rationale: The x86-64 port already found the per-CPU boundary the hard way: the interrupted stack pointer is per-thread, not per-CPU, and a global looked right until one core disproved it. docs/smp.md now counts what SMP would actually take rather than guessing.

nodes.label: PowerPC (wanted)
nodes.rationale: The first big-endian target, and the audit for that was done and holds. A G4 is 32-bit, which contradicts a principle and so gets decided rather than drifted past.

nodes.label: There are no milestones (there were thirteen)
nodes.rationale: A number that no longer means anything is worse than no number, because it is read as though it does: the README said 'M6, graphics' while the machine had a journalled filesystem, a TCP/IP stack and a web browser in it. roadmap.md is two lists now - what is built and what is wanted.
